content.p: Derek Ernest Percy was never convicted of a crime in the ordinary sense. After the 1969 killing a Victorian jury found him not guilty by reason of insanity of murdering 12-year-old Yvonne Tuohy, and he was detained indefinitely. He then spent more than four decades behind bars, and for much of that time police, journalists and bereaved families believed he was responsible for other children's deaths across Australia. He died in July 2013 without charge in any of those cases. Fifteen months later a Victorian coroner found that he had caused the death of one of them, seven-year-old Linda Stilwell.

The case is a study in how far a suspicion can travel without a trial. Percy denied involvement in Linda Stilwell's disappearance from his hospital bed days before he died, and for several of them the evidence remains circumstantial or, in the view of some writers, thin.

According to the Seven Network's Sunday Night program in 2011, Percy's family moved repeatedly, and he went to five schools and lived out his teens at Mount Beauty, in the hills of north-east Victoria. The program described his father as distant and domineering and his mother as controlling. The program's narrator said that at 16 Percy was caught stealing women's underwear and slashing it with a knife, and that he was expelled from school after an assault on two six-year-old girls for which no charges were laid. The family moved again.

At 19 he joined the navy. Fellow sailors found him secretive and private, and called him "The Spook". The journalist Debi Marshall, author of the book Lambs to the Slaughter, told the program that she had spent five years tracing where Percy had been at the time of notorious child crimes, and that she believed he used leave from the navy, and earlier holidays, to hunt children. That is her view, offered in a television documentary, and not a finding of any court.

The one crime for which Percy was tried took place on a beach at Warneet, on Victoria's Westernport Bay, in July 1969. Yvonne Tuohy was there with a friend, Shane Spiller. Murderpedia's collection of news reports says that Percy, then a 21-year-old naval rating, seized Yvonne and held a knife to her throat. In Spiller's own words, broadcast in a newsreel, the man warned him to put down the tomahawk he had pulled from his belt "or else I'll hurt the girl". Spiller ran to the main road and stopped a passing car. Yvonne was heard calling for help as he fled.

Spiller remembered a navy sticker on the back of the attacker's car. Police followed it to the Cerberus naval base, where, according to Marshall, they found Percy washing blood from his clothes. He first denied all knowledge, she said, until conceding that he had been on the beach. The Murderpedia account says a detective sergeant took him back through the day until he could say where he had left the body, about ten kilometres from the beach.

Ron Anderson, by now a probationary constable, was asked by homicide detectives to speak to his old schoolmate in the cells. He later said Percy was sobbing on a bed. When Anderson raised the Beaumont children, Percy said he had been in Adelaide at the time and recalled only "The beach, that's all". About Linda Stilwell, Percy said he had driven from Portsea through St Kilda to a club for drinks on the day. Anderson gave his notes to detectives; he said no action followed on the other cases.

In his naval locker, the Sunday Night program reported, police found handwritten notes setting out plans to abduct and harm children. The jury, which saw photographs of Yvonne's injuries, found him not guilty by reason of insanity. Marshall's explanation was that the jurors could not accept that a sane person had done such a thing, and that the verdict also spared him the gallows, since the death penalty then existed. He was committed to Ararat Hospital in April 1970, according to Murderpedia.
Over the years Percy's name was attached to a series of unsolved cases. Each is described below with who linked him to it and what is, and is not, established.

Wanda Beach, January 1965. Christine Sharrock and Marianne Schmidt, two friends from Ryde in Sydney, were separated from Marianne's younger siblings during an afternoon at the beach. ABC News reported that they were stabbed and bashed to death and partly buried in the dunes, and that their bodies were found the next day. Reports differ on the date and on the girls' ages; the ABC gave 11 January and most reports say 15. No one has been charged. Percy's grandmother lived in Ryde, and Marshall said a witness described a thin-faced young man who chatted to the girls on the train. Percy was 16. The author Alan Whiticker, who has written on both the Wanda Beach and Beaumont cases, told the ABC the Victorian police placement of Percy in Sydney was a strong coincidence, and that the 1969 injuries matched the Wanda Beach scenario, but he thought the Beaumont link weaker.

The Beaumont children, January 1966. Jane, Arnna and Grant Beaumont took a bus to Glenelg Beach near Adelaide on the morning of 26 January 1966 and never came home. ABC News said a bus driver confirmed seeing them, but there were no other confirmed sightings, despite a reward of 500 pounds, and enquiries that drew in both the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Scotland Yard, and many leads. Percy admitted he was in Adelaide on a family holiday. At a 1969 police interview he was asked if he had killed the children and answered, according to InDaily: "I could have killed them, I don't remember a thing." South Australia Police told the ABC in 2013 that it had never treated him as a significant person of interest. Whiticker questioned whether a teenager on holiday with his parents could have hidden three children.

Allen Redston, September 1966. Allen was a six-year-old sent to buy ice cream in the Canberra suburb of Curtin. According to the Australian Federal Police, his body was found beside a creek, bound and wrapped in a carpet and a dressing gown. In 2003 detectives named an unidentified man as a suspect but could not establish a link. The Sunday Night program noted only that Percy was on a family holiday in Canberra that year and owned a red bicycle like one ridden by the suspect.

Simon Brook, May 1968. Three-year-old Simon was last seen walking away from the front yard of his Glebe home with a thin-faced man. His body was found the next day on a building site beside an orphanage. Percy was stationed at the Garden Island dockyard, about three kilometres away, and told police in 1969 that he had driven past the site that day. ABC News reported that details in one of Percy's diaries allegedly matched the injuries. A second inquest, held in 2005, advised that Percy's file go to the prosecuting authority. The Director of Public Prosecutions at the time, Nicholas Cowdery, judged the evidence insufficient. The program also featured a man who as a boy had lived in the orphanage; he said he saw Percy near the gates and later holding the hand of a toddler. Reports differ on the day of the killing, 18 or 19 May.

Linda Stilwell, August 1968. The seven-year-old vanished from a penny arcade at Luna Park, St Kilda, where she was with her brother Gary, then nine. A witness reported seeing a girl leave with a thin-faced man. Another woman said she saw Linda near a man in a dark spray jacket, and Percy was photographed in a jacket of that style after his 1969 arrest. This was the case in which a coroner found Percy responsible.

As a prisoner, Percy appears to have been orderly. Murderpedia quotes a prison officer who called him "the chess champion, a stamp collector" and a good tennis player, but also "our Hannibal Lecter". In 1998 his case went before Justice Geoffrey Eames, because new rules applied to prisoners held at the Governor's pleasure. On 30 September 1998 Eames refused to set a minimum term or release date, although Percy had passed the 25 years usual for such prisoners. He said Percy had never sought or been given treatment and "has demonstrated no significant remorse or anxiety, at least none which I find credible". Justice Murray Kellam refused a request in March 2004 to move him to the Thomas Embling psychiatric hospital. A report quoted by Murderpedia, apparently the one leaked to the Herald Sun, said Percy did not have a mental illness, though he had a personality disorder and "sadistic fantasy life" involving children. In 2005 the Victorian opposition leader, Robert Doyle, called for laws to keep prisoners like him locked up for life, and Attorney-General Rob Hulls replied that the state could already imprison dangerous offenders indefinitely.

The 2011 program reported that the Supreme Court of Victoria had re-examined his sanity the year before and found he suffered from no identifiable psychiatric disorder. Professor Donald Brook, Simon's father, argued that because Percy had not been convicted of any crime he might one day win parole.

In August 2007, after 35 boxes of documents were found in a South Melbourne storage unit, Victoria Police were granted eight hours to question Percy, who was 57. John Silvester of The Age told ABC radio that the papers dated from the 1970s and included diary entries and a cartoon with the word "Wanda" in handwriting, which police thought linked to the Wanda Beach killings. There was also a 1978 street directory with marks towards St Kilda Pier, packets of razor blades similar to those used on one of the victims, and diary entries that seemed to echo events in several unsolved cases. Chief Commissioner Christine Nixon could not explain how a prisoner had sent boxes out for more than 30 years. Silvester noted that, since Percy had been found sane, he could in theory stand trial on other cases if there were enough evidence.

In 2009 the coroner, Iain West, issued an interim finding placing Percy in the St Kilda area on the day Linda vanished. He then chose not to compel Percy to give evidence, citing concern it would be unreliable. Victoria's highest court overturned that decision and reconvened the inquest. Percy gave evidence from his hospital bed on the Saturday before his death, denying involvement and saying he had "no idea" where she could be found. He died overnight, a death reported on 24 July 2013, and Corrections Victoria gave his age as 64. It said his death would go to the coroner. Linda's brother Gary Stilwell said he was disappointed that Percy had taken his secrets to the grave.

On 29 October 2014 West found that Linda was dead and that Percy had caused her death. The coroner called the evidence implicating him circumstantial but said it was "highly unlikely that another child molester was in the vicinity when Linda disappeared". Detective Senior Sergeant Wayne Newman said police had begun by trying to rule Percy out, and could not. Linda's mother, Jean Priest, said she hoped her daughter's remains would one day be found. A non-publication order from 2009 limited what the ABC could report of the ruling.
